key_clinical_evidence: Recurrent stereotyped focal impaired-awareness seizures over 18 months, two of them progressing to bilateral convulsions, meet the definition of epilepsy [ILAE_def_2014]; she has never taken an antiseizure medication, so the epilepsy is not drug-resistant.

The dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI with thin coronal sequences shows a left anteroinferior temporal encephalocele through a middle cranial fossa floor defect with normal hippocampi; the earlier standard axial 1.5T MRI did not show it.

Localization rests on concordance of the EEG (left anterior temporal discharges and video-EEG ictal onset at F7/T3), the MRI lesion at the left temporal pole, and postictal expressive language difficulty in a right-handed woman; unilateral right-hand automatisms do not by themselves lateralize to the left.
CT with bone windows shows the 5.2 mm defect of the left greater sphenoid wing for surgical planning.

Mildly blurred discs without spontaneous venous pulsations, pulsatile tinnitus, partial empty sella and obesity are features associated with temporal encephaloceles; they do not cause the focal seizures but need formal neuro-ophthalmic assessment.
Video-EEG capture of habitual events with an ictal correlate refutes the earlier attribution to panic disorder.

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Reyes is a 41-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman with obesity and chronic headaches who is admitted to the epilepsy monitoring unit for evaluation of recurrent stereotyped paroxysmal episodes over approximately 18 months. Episodes begin with a brief olfactory sensation (burning rubber) followed by a rising epigastric sensation lasting 5-10 seconds, then loss of awareness with blank staring, lip-smacking, and rhythmic right-hand automatisms lasting 60-90 seconds, followed by 3-5 minutes of confusion and mild expressive language difficulty. She has no memory of the events. Frequency was one per month initially but has increased to 3-4 per month over the past six months. On two occasions, both after sleep deprivation, an episode progressed to a generalized convulsion witnessed by her husband. She has not been told to stop driving but has stopped driving on her own.

Ten months ago her primary care physician obtained a routine 1.5T brain MRI without contrast (standard axial protocol, no thin coronal sequences) that was reported as 'no acute intracranial abnormality, normal study.' She was reassured and not referred to neurology. Her family physician subsequently attributed the episodes to anxiety and panic disorder given chronic headaches and occasional palpitations; sertraline 50 mg was started one month ago but self-discontinued after two weeks due to nausea without symptomatic benefit. She has never taken an antiseizure medication.

Past history is notable for obesity, longstanding tension-type headaches (2-3 times per week over 5 years), and episodic left-ear pulsatile tinnitus attributed to eustachian tube dysfunction. No prior epilepsy diagnosis.

A neurologist acquaintance who witnessed one of her events at a community meeting advised a neurological evaluation, and she was referred for admission for a structured epilepsy work-up.

No tongue biting or urinary incontinence with habitual events.
